result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.largest_common_subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Find the largest induced subgraphs that this graph and another have in common. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.largest_common_subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Find the largest induced subgraphs that this graph and another have in common. title: >- [Graph.largest_common_subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Find the largest induced subgraphs that this graph and another have in common. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the largest induced subgraphs that this graph and another have in common. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L21153-L21260){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.largest_common_subgraph( other, symmetry=True, node_attr=None, edge_attr=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Largest common subgraph](/assets/graphs/largest-common-subgraph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: graph square, the 4-cycle a, b, c, d, beside graph paw, a triangle x, y, z with a pendant w on z. The biggest induced subgraph they share is a path of three nodes, found 8 ways. The first match is in the accent color in both graphs: x maps to b, z to a and w to d, so the path x, z, w lands on b, a, d. y stays faint; its path is a symmetric copy of x's, so it isn't listed again." width="100%"} A common induced subgraph is a set of nodes of `other` whose induced subgraph (the nodes with every edge among them) also appears, as an induced subgraph, in this graph. This method finds the largest such node sets and returns every way of matching them. Comparing two molecules, two versions of a network, or a query against a database graph by their largest shared structure gives a similarity that, unlike an exact subgraph search, still says something when neither graph contains the other. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The `Graph` to compare with. It is not modified. Both graphs must have the same directedness. [symmetry]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), mappings that differ only by an automorphism of `other` are reported once (see `subgraph_isomorphisms()`). If `False`, every mapping is listed. [node_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | list[str] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional node attribute name, or list of names, whose values must be equal for matched nodes. [edge_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | list[str] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional edge attribute name, or list of names, whose values must be equal for matched edges. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[dict[int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : One dictionary per largest common subgraph, mapping node IDs of `other` to node IDs of this graph. All have the same size. If `other` has no nodes, the one empty mapping; if this graph has none, an empty list. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If one graph is directed and the other is not. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} This is the largest common subgraph search of ISMAGS (Houbraken et al., 2014), as in NetworkX's `ISMAGS(G, other).largest_common_subgraph()`: `other` is first matched whole, as an induced subgraph, into this graph; if it doesn't occur, every subset with one node fewer is tried, and so on, until some subset occurs. With `symmetry=True`, the constraints of `subgraph_isomorphisms(..., symmetry=True)` prune the matches, and a removed node whose coset holds a larger node still in the subset is swapped for it, so symmetric subsets are tried once. The mappings go from `other` to this graph, the reverse of NetworkX's graph-to-subgraph dictionaries. The problem is NP-hard and the number of subsets grows exponentially as the common part shrinks, so this suits small graphs, or graphs that share most of their structure. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A square and a triangle with a pendant share a path of three nodes, and nothing larger: ::: {#a496fa80 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec square = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["a", "b", "c", "d"]) square.add_edges([("a", "b"), ("b", "c"), ("c", "d"), ("d", "a")]) paw = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["x", "y", "z", "w"]) paw.add_edges([("x", "y"), ("y", "z"), ("z", "x"), ("z", "w")]) found = square.largest_common_subgraph(paw) len(found) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 8 ``` ::: ::: The 8 matches are the square's 4 three-node paths, each run in both directions, laid onto the path `x`-`z`-`w` (the path from `y` is a symmetric copy, so it is skipped): ::: {#27b1924f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} {paw.get_label_from_id(k): square.get_label_from_id(v) for k, v in found[0].items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'x': 'b', 'z': 'a', 'w': 'd'} ``` ::: :::
